doc.title: Tom Malone interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, May 3, 2023

title: Gladys Knight Christmas album and the wrong Ave Maria
summary: A 48-piece orchestra session where the wrong Ave Maria was arranged and everyone transposed on the spot; Malone reads any horn part on any horn.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Speaking of that, have you been in sessions where there was an ad person, you know a commercial, and the ad person and the producer may be one and the same, that made tempers flare somewhat?
There’s always someone that can cause anxiety, yes. And you never know what’s going to happen in the studio. So you can’t, you know you have to be iron clad. You have to

have a defense mechanism against anything that would ordinarily make you angry. You can’t — you don’t have time in a session to get angry. Oh here’s a story you might enjoy. Gladys Knight and the Pips Christmas album. A 48-piece orchestra in the studio, and so we spent at least the first two hours just rehearsing and getting the mix correct, getting the sounds and everything correct. So then we started in on the songs and we had all the songs done except one. There were three songs we were recording. Okay? So now we have one more song to do and we have about 15 minutes left on the session. And okay, “Ave Maria.” So the conductor counts off and we start in to the song and in the booth they go, “Cut it off, cut it off.” And they called the conductor back in to the — conductor/arranger — they called him back into the control room and you see there’s some commotion going on in there. Well it turns out there are two different songs called “Ave Maria.”

And so he arranged the wrong “Ave Maria.” Okay? So now there’s a lot of commotion in there. So they decide to record this version of “Ave Maria.” And Gladys Knight is in there so they figure out what key she should do it in so now there’s five minutes left in the session. There’s time for one take. And the conductor walks in and he says, “‘Ave Maria’ down a fourth. One-two-three-four.” And that’s the one that’s on the record. Everybody transposed it instantaneously.

Wow. I’m speechless. You know for — I play alto so I’m pretty good at you know, up a minor third from concert, etcetera, or you know tenor down, but that’s really something. It reminds me of Frank Wess who would play tenor parts on his alto with Basie ‘cause he was too lazy to pick up the other horn or whatever, and he just did that.

Well I can do that, I can read an alto part on tenor and vice versa, tenor part on alto. I can read a trumpet part on the trombone. I can read a baritone part — I can do that too. Being an arranger you know I can read any horn part on any other, yeah, just because I’ve been doing it so long.
